## Candidal and Dermatophyte Nail Involvement

Candidal onychomycosis is characterized by invasion of pseudohyphae throughout the entire nail plate, adjacent cuticle, granular layer, and stratum spinosum of the nail bed, as well as the hyponychial stratum corneum. In contrast, dermatophyte infections show a predilection for the ventral nail and nail bed stratum corneum. ### <mark>Tinea Capitis/Favus</mark>

<mark>Multiple systemic and topical antifungal agents are effective against dermatophytes.</mark> <mark>Infections involving hair-bearing skin require oral therapy due to fungal invasion of the hair follicle.</mark>

#### <mark>Griseofulvin</mark>
<mark>Griseofulvin remains the only oral antifungal approved by the U.S.</mark> <mark>Food and Drug Administration for tinea capitis.</mark> <mark>The traditional pediatric dose was 10–20 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks, administered with a fatty meal to enhance absorption.</mark> <mark>However, due to reported high failure rates, current expert recommendations favor higher doses: 20–25 mg/kg/day of the microsize formulation or 15 mg/kg/day of the ultramicrosize formulation, given for 8 weeks—though this is not based on controlled clinical trials.</mark>

<mark>Disadvantages include poor compliance due to treatment duration and cost, bitter taste in liquid form, photosensitivity, headache, and gastrointestinal side effects.</mark> <mark>Griseofulvin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P₄₅₀ enzymes.</mark> <mark>Routine laboratory monitoring is not required for standard treatment courses.</mark>

#### <mark>Fluconazole</mark>
<mark>Available in both tablet and palatable liquid forms, fluconazole at 6 mg/kg/day for 20 days achieves an 89% cure rate in *Trichophyton tonsurans* tinea capitis.</mark> <mark>Alternative regimens include weekly dosing of 8 mg/kg for 8–16 weeks or 6 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks, followed by a single week of retreatment 4 weeks later if clinically indicated.</mark>

<mark>Fluconazole absorption is unaffected by food, and gastrointestinal side effects are uncommon.</mark> <mark>Hepatotoxicity has been reported but is less frequent than with ketoconazole.</mark>

#### <mark>Itraconazole</mark>
<mark>At doses of 3–5 mg/kg/day, itraconazole effectively clears tinea capitis caused by *Microsporum* or *Trichophyton* species within 4–6 weeks.</mark> <mark>Pulse therapy (5 mg/kg/day for 1 week per month, repeated for 1–3 cycles) is also effective.</mark>

<mark>Terbinafine at 3–6 mg/kg/day cures *Trichophyton* tinea capitis in 2–4 weeks, but 4–8 weeks are needed for *Microsporum* infections.</mark> A randomized trial comparing 4 weeks of terbinafine to 8 weeks of griseofulvin showed no overall significant difference in efficacy. # <mark>CONGENITAL ICHTHYOSIFORM ERYTHRODERMA</mark>

<mark>Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE) is apparent at birth, with affected newborns typically presenting with a taut, shiny **collodion membrane**.</mark> <mark>After the membrane sheds, the skin remains diffusely red and is covered with a fine, white, generalized scale (see Fig.</mark> 47-5). <mark>On the lower legs, the scale may become larger and darker.</mark> In contrast to lamellar ichthyosis, classic CIE usually lacks significant **ectropion**, **eclabium**, or **alopecia**.

Sweating capacity varies widely; many infants and children with CIE have **minimal sweating** and exhibit **severe heat intolerance**. Mucous membranes are generally spared. Palmoplantar involvement is variable—some patients show mild thickening, while others have normal palms and soles. Nails may develop **ridging**, but are often unaffected. As with all forms of ichthyosis, there is an increased risk of **dermatophyte infections** of the skin and nails.

Histopathologically, CIE is characterized by **hyperkeratosis**, **acanthosis**, and frequent **parakeratosis** (see Fig. 47-2C). <mark>Studies have demonstrated **markedly increased epidermal cell turnover**, which contrasts with the slower turnover seen in lamellar ichthyosis.[49]</mark>

Genetically, CIE is part of the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) spectrum. A small subset of patients with CIE have mutations in the **$TGM1$** gene. Additionally, two siblings with a mixed phenotype—CIE and palmoplantar keratoderma—were found to have an autosomal dominant mutation in **loricrin**, a cornified envelope protein.[54] Genetic heterogeneity in ARCI is well established: **$TGM1$** has been excluded as the causative gene in some families with classic lamellar ichthyosis or CIE phenotypes, and mutations in other genes have been identified.

To date, mutations in **five additional genes** have been linked to nonsyndromic ARCI, and **two more** to syndromic forms. Two genetic loci—**12p11.2-q13** and **19p13.1-13.2**—are associated with ARCI, though the responsible genes remain unidentified (Table 47-3). A newly proposed **lipoxygenase pathway** may serve as a unifying mechanism linking many forms of ARCI.[20] However, this hypothesis requires further validation, and the connection between the most common ARCI mutation (**$TGM1$**) and lipid abnormalities remains unclear.

---

# EPIDERMOLYTIC HYPERKERATOSIS

In 1902, Brocq described **bullous ichthyotic erythroderma**, distinguishing the blistering form from nonblistering congenital ichthyotic erythroderma.[55] His report included three unrelated patients with variable clinical features, likely representing the first documented cases of what is now known as **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis** (OMIM #113800).

The condition is named for its hallmark histopathologic findings: **vacuolar degeneration** of the epidermis (epidermal lysis) and **hyperkeratosis**. It is also referred to as **bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma**, a descriptive term highlighting the neonatal onset of blistering, erythema, scaling, and erosions.

Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis follows an **autosomal dominant** inheritance pattern, with an estimated prevalence of **1 in 200,000 to 300,000** individuals. However, **spontaneous mutations** are common, accounting for up to **50% of cases**, which therefore lack a family history.

Clinically, the disease presents at birth with **widespread blistering**, **erythema**, and **skin peeling** (Fig. 47-6).

# <mark>ICHTHYOSIS</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>A heterogeneous group of skin diseases characterized by generalized scaling and, often, areas of thickened skin.</mark>  
Most types are inherited and usually present at birth; however, some forms are acquired.  
Scales may vary in size, color, and distribution across the body.  
May be accompanied by erythema, abnormalities of the skin adnexa, and other cutaneous findings.  
Can be associated with systemic manifestations such as failure to thrive, increased susceptibility to infection, atopic dermatitis, neurosensory deafness, and neurologic disorders.  
Histopathology is typically non-specific, except in conditions such as epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, neutral lipid storage disease, Refsum disease, and acquired ichthyosis associated with sarcoidosis.

---

## <mark>OVERVIEW</mark>

Early reports of ichthyosis in Indian and Chinese medical literature date back several hundred years B.C. The condition was later described by Robert Willan in 1808.

Ichthyosis may present at birth or develop later in life. It can be limited to the skin or occur in association with abnormalities in other organ systems. While several well-defined types of ichthyosis can be reliably diagnosed based on clinical and genetic features, the significant clinical heterogeneity and the influence of environmental factors on scaling can make specific diagnosis challenging in some patients and families.

Siemens introduced genetic concepts into the classification of ichthyoses, laying the foundation for modern understanding.

Advances in genetic research have identified the underlying gene defects in many forms of ichthyosis—classified as genodermatoses. A new classification system is emerging, based on molecular and genetic etiologies. Identifying the mutated gene provides insight into the pathophysiologic mechanism, enabling more rational approaches to diagnosis, classification, and treatment.

Grouping these disorders by inheritance pattern (Table 47-1) and by underlying molecular abnormality (Table 47-2) enhances understanding of their clinical phenotypes and disease mechanisms. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate how specific gene mutations and protein disruptions lead to clinical disease, and to develop targeted, innovative therapies.

## <mark>X-LINKED ICHTHYOSIS</mark>

Serum cholesterol sulfate levels are typically elevated in X-linked ichthyosis (2000 to 9000 μg/dL), compared to the normal range of 80 to 200 μg/dL. Unfortunately, cholesterol sulfate determination in serum and skin scales may not be readily available for laboratory confirmation. In rare cases where deletions are not detected but clinical suspicion remains high, arylsulfatase C (steroid sulfatase) enzyme activity can be measured in cultured fibroblasts.  

Deletions involving adjacent sulfatase genes can explain overlap syndromes that include chondrodysplasia punctata and X-linked ichthyosis. Additionally, X-linked Kallmann syndrome—characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, anosmia, and sometimes renal abnormalities, obesity, synkinesis, cleft palate, and spastic paraplegia—can co-occur with X-linked recessive ichthyosis as part of a contiguous gene deletion syndrome.  

Because of this association and the increased risk of testicular carcinoma, patients with X-linked recessive ichthyosis should be questioned about anosmia and undergo periodic testicular examinations.

In the epidermis, steroid sulfatase catalyzes the hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate. The deficiency of this enzyme in X-linked ichthyosis underscores the importance of cholesterol sulfate hydrolysis in normal desquamation. Topical application of cholesterol sulfate in mice induces a scaling disorder, further supporting its role in corneocyte shedding.

A family has been described with an X-linked inheritance pattern for ichthyosis but with normal steroid sulfatase activity and absence of corneal opacities. This finding demonstrates genetic heterogeneity within X-linked ichthyosis. Although steroid sulfatase deficiency accounts for the majority of cases, a normal enzyme level in a male with ichthyosis does not exclude X-linked inheritance.

---

## <mark>AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE CONGENITAL ICHTHYOSIS (ARCI)</mark>

Autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) is a heterogeneous group of disorders presenting at birth with generalized skin involvement. ARCI may be syndromic (associated with extracutaneous manifestations) or nonsyndromic. It is rare, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 300,000 individuals.

Historically, non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (NCIE) and lamellar ichthyosis (both autosomal recessive) were distinguished from bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, autosomal dominant) based on clinical features such as the presence of bullae and inheritance pattern. However, the interchangeable use of "lamellar ichthyosis" with NCIE—and the inclusion of a spectrum of phenotypes under this term—has led to diagnostic confusion.

Williams and Elias differentiated lamellar ichthyosis from congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE), the latter being a milder, erythrodermic form. <mark>Clinically, lamellar ichthyosis is characterized by large, dark, plate-like scales.</mark> Although affected infants may be erythrodermic at birth, adults typically show less redness and more prominent scaling compared to those with CIE.

# <mark>Sezary Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>DEFINITION</mark>  
<mark>Sezary Syndrome (SS) is a leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) that occurs exclusively in adults.</mark> It is characterized by the triad of diffuse erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells with cerebriform nuclei, known as Sezary cells.

## CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS  
<mark>Clinical findings include severe scaling or fissuring of the palms and soles, alopecia, and onychodystrophy.</mark> <mark>The erythroderma may be associated with marked exfoliation, edema, and lichenification, and is typically extremely pruritic.</mark>

## LABORATORY FINDINGS  
SS demonstrates histologic features similar to those of mycosis fungoides (MF). According to diagnostic criteria proposed by the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphoma and incorporated into the WHO-EORTC classification, diagnosis requires:  
- Skin biopsy findings consistent with CTCL  
- Absolute Sezary cell count in peripheral blood ≥1000 cells/mm³  
- Peripheral blood flow cytometry showing:  
  - CD4/CD8 ratio >10  
  - Loss of CD7 expression in >40% of T cells (CD7⁻ phenotype)  
  - Evidence of a clonal circulating T-cell population  

Patients who lack definitive peripheral blood atypia or clonal evidence are classified as having erythrodermic CTCL rather than SS.

## TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS  
Compared to patients with patch- or plaque-stage mycosis fungoides, those with SS have a significantly worse prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of approximately 33%. By the time SS manifests, there is often profound immunosuppression. Many patients die from infectious complications rather than from progressive lymphoma.

---

# Primary Cutaneous CD30⁺ Lymphoproliferative Disorders

Primary cutaneous CD30⁺ lymphoproliferative disorders encompass lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) and cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (cALCL). These entities are now recognized as representing a spectrum, with some cases showing overlapping features that make definitive classification based on histomorphology alone challenging.

## LYMPHOMATOID PAPULOSIS

### Definition  
Lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) was first described by Macaulay in 1968. It is an uncommon, chronic disorder (incidence: 1.2–1.9 cases per 1,000,000) characterized by recurrent, self-healing crops of papules and papulonodules.

### Clinical Manifestations  
Patients develop disseminated, recurrent papules and papulonodules that may become necrotic or ulcerate centrally.

# <mark>Apocrine Bromhidrosis</mark>

<mark>Apocrine secretions are responsible for odor production, primarily through bacterial action on their components.</mark> <mark>The axilla hosts a diverse microbiome, predominantly composed of gram-positive bacteria.</mark> <mark>Odor formation in apocrine bromhidrosis is particularly associated with aerobic *Corynebacterium* species.</mark> <mark>Odorous steroids, including **16-androstenes**, **$5\alpha$-androstenol**, and **$5\alpha$-androstenone**, are known contributors to the characteristic malodor of bromhidrosis.[3,4] The biotransformation of these steroids involves complex metabolic pathways that are not yet fully understood and require further research.[3,4]</mark>

<mark>Bacterial degradation of apocrine secretions yields **ammonia** and **short-chain fatty acids**.</mark> <mark>The most well-characterized of these is **$\varepsilon$-3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid**, which is transported to the skin surface bound to two specific proteins: **apocrine secretion-binding proteins (ASOB1 and ASOB2)**.</mark> <mark>ASOB2 has been identified as **apolipoprotein D**.[5,6]</mark>

<mark>**$5\alpha$-Reductase type I** is expressed in apocrine glands, and individuals with bromhidrosis exhibit increased levels of this enzyme.</mark> <mark>Since $5\alpha$-reductase catalyzes the conversion of **testosterone** to **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**, affected individuals may have higher DHT concentrations than testosterone in the skin.</mark>

<mark>The role of **hyperhidrosis** (excessive eccrine sweating) in apocrine bromhidrosis remains unclear.</mark> <mark>Some suggest that increased eccrine sweat may reduce odor by flushing out apocrine secretions.</mark> <mark>Conversely, others propose that eccrine sweat exacerbates bromhidrosis by spreading apocrine components across the skin and maintaining a moist environment conducive to bacterial proliferation.[2]</mark>

---

## <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

### <mark>History</mark>
<mark>Patients typically report an unpleasant body odor.</mark> <mark>The **axillae** are the most commonly affected site, though involvement of the **genital area** or **plantar surface of the feet** can also occur.</mark> <mark>Diagnosis is primarily clinical.</mark> <mark>Perception of "normal" body odor varies widely among individuals and ethnic groups.</mark> <mark>In some Asian populations, even mild odor may be considered abnormal or diagnostic.[8,9]</mark>

### <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>
<mark>Physical examination is usually unremarkable, with no visible skin changes.</mark>

### <mark>Laboratory Tests</mark>
<mark>No laboratory abnormalities are associated with apocrine bromhidrosis.</mark>

### <mark>Pathology</mark>
<mark>Findings are variable.</mark> <mark>Some studies report no structural abnormalities in apocrine glands, while others describe an **increase in the number and size** of apocrine glands in affected individuals.[8]</mark>

---

## Differential Diagnosis

Apocrine bromhidrosis must be distinguished from **eccrine bromhidrosis**, which is less common (see Chap. 82). Eccrine sweat is generally **odorless**, widely distributed, and functions in thermoregulation. Eccrine bromhidrosis may arise from bacterial breakdown of **keratin softened by sweat**, and is typically localized to the **plantar feet**. Contributing factors include certain **foods** (e.g., garlic, curry, alcohol), **drugs** (e.g., bromides), **toxins**, or **metabolic disorders** (e.g., amino acid metabolism defects).

---

## Treatment

### General Measures
- Frequent washing of the axillae  
- Use of **deodorants** or **antiperspirants** (e.g., aluminum chloride)  
- Maintaining good hygiene to reduce bacterial load

## <mark>Apocrine-Eccrine Hybrid Glands and Apocrine Sweat Glands</mark>

### <mark>Apocrine-Eccrine Hybrid Glands (AEGs)</mark>

The relative frequency of apocrine-eccrine hybrid glands (AEGs) varies widely among adults. In individuals with axillary hyperhidrosis, up to 50% of axillary sweat glands—comprising eccrine, apocrine, and hybrid types—are of the apocrine type. In contrast, individuals without axillary hyperhidrosis show a much lower proportion of AEGs.

Like eccrine glands, AEGs possess a long duct that opens directly onto the skin surface, differing from true apocrine glands, whose ducts open into hair follicles. The secretory tubule of the AEG consists of two segments: a narrow segment with a diameter less than 80 μm (similar to the eccrine secretory tubule) and a second segment that undergoes uniform or irregular dilatation, reaching up to 500 μm in diameter. These segments are functionally connected, as demonstrated by micropuncture studies.

The thick segment of the AEG closely resembles the secretory portion of the apocrine gland, although some columnar secretory cells contain abundant mitochondria. The thin segment is histologically indistinguishable from the eccrine secretory coil. Functionally, the AEG responds to both cholinergic and adrenergic stimulation. Its secretory rate can be up to 10 times greater than that of eccrine glands, primarily due to its larger size, suggesting a potential role in axillary hyperhidrosis.

Notably, the AEG responds equally well to epinephrine and methacholine, indicating dual receptor sensitivity. It has been proposed that the AEG may represent an eccrine gland that has undergone "apocrinization" under the influence of local growth factors. If this hypothesis is correct, similar apocrinization processes might occur elsewhere in the body where such factors are present.

---

### <mark>Apocrine Sweat Glands</mark>

<mark>In addition to eccrine and apocrine-eccrine hybrid glands, true apocrine sweat glands are present in humans, predominantly located in the axillae and perineum.</mark> <mark>These glands become functionally active just before puberty, suggesting hormonal regulation during sexual maturation, although the specific hormones involved have not been definitively identified.</mark> <mark>Notably, gonadectomy in mature individuals does not impair apocrine gland function, indicating that while their development is hormone-dependent, the maintenance of their activity is not.</mark> <mark>Thus, if classified as secondary sex characteristics, it is their development—not ongoing function—that relies on sex hormones.</mark>

#### <mark>Functions</mark>

<mark>Apocrine glands have been associated with several proposed functions, including:</mark>
- <mark>Production of odoriferous substances that may act as sexual attractants</mark>
- <mark>Territorial marking</mark>
- <mark>Warning signals</mark>
- <mark>Enhancement of frictional resistance and tactile sensitivity</mark>
- <mark>Contribution to evaporative heat loss in some nonhuman species</mark>

<mark>Pheromone production by apocrine glands is well documented in many animal species.</mark> <mark>Given that human apocrine glands become active at puberty and produce odorous secretions after bacterial modification, it is plausible—though speculative—that they once served a sexual or social signaling role that may now be vestigial.</mark>

High levels of **15-lipoxygenase-2** are found in the secretory cells of human apocrine glands. This enzyme produces **15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (15-HETE)**, a ligand for the nuclear receptor **peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-γ)**, which may function as a signaling molecule involved in secretion or cellular differentiation.

In nonhuman furred primates, apocrine glands may also contribute to thermoregulation.

#### Composition of Secretion

Human apocrine sweat is initially milky, viscous, and odorless when secreted. Odor develops only after bacterial degradation on the skin. The precise chemical composition of human apocrine secretion remains poorly understood, primarily due to challenges in collecting pure samples uncontaminated by eccrine sweat.

Moreover, because apocrine glands often share a ductal opening with sebaceous glands (forming a sudosebaceous canal), their secretions mix with sebum. This admixture likely accounts for the milky appearance of fluid collected via duct cannulation.

#### Mode of Secretion

Cannulation studies of the human apocrine sweat gland duct have revealed that secretion occurs in a pulsatile manner. This pulsatility is believed to result from contractions of the myoepithelial cells that surround the secretory epithelium, facilitating the expulsion of secretory product.

# <mark>Disorders of the Apocrine Sweat Glands</mark>

Marni C. Wiseman

<mark>Apocrine glands are adnexal glands distributed in the axillae, anogenital region, Moll's glands of the eyelid, ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus, and mammary glands.</mark> <mark>They may also be found in limited numbers on the face and abdomen.</mark> <mark>These glands remain quiescent until puberty.</mark> Embryologically, apocrine glands develop from the upper bulge of the hair follicle during the late fourth month of gestation, with continued development coinciding with hair follicle formation. <mark>Structurally, apocrine glands consist of three parts: the intraepithelial duct, the intradermal duct, and the secretory portion.</mark>

<mark>Four conditions are discussed in this chapter: **apocrine bromhidrosis**, **apocrine chromhidrosis**, **Fox-Fordyce disease**, and **hidradenitis suppurativa**.</mark> <mark>It is important to note that Fox-Fordyce disease and hidradenitis suppurativa are not primary disorders of apocrine glands; rather, apocrine glands become secondarily involved in these conditions.</mark>

---

## <mark>Apocrine Bromhidrosis</mark>

<mark>**Bromhidrosis** refers to malodorous body odor, a common occurrence in postpubertal individuals.</mark> <mark>When the odor becomes excessive or particularly offensive, it is termed **apocrine bromhidrosis**, which originates from apocrine gland secretions—most commonly in the axillae.</mark> <mark>This condition can significantly impair psychosocial functioning.</mark> <mark>The terms *bromhidrosis* and *osmidrosis* are often used interchangeably, though some sources define *osmidrosis* as offensive odor and *bromhidrosis* as osmidrosis occurring in conjunction with hyperhidrosis.</mark>

---

### <mark>Epidemiology</mark>

<mark>Onset typically occurs after puberty and is more prevalent among African American populations.</mark> <mark>There is no specific geographic predilection, although symptoms may worsen during summer months or in warm climates.</mark> <mark>Poor personal hygiene can exacerbate the condition.</mark> <mark>A familial tendency has been observed, particularly in individuals of Far Eastern descent.</mark>

---

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>Apocrine glands are most densely concentrated in the axillae and genital region, with additional presence in the breasts, ears (ceruminous glands), and periorbital areas (Moll’s glands).</mark> <mark>The characteristic odor in bromhidrosis results from bacterial degradation of apocrine secretions.</mark>

<mark>The axillary microbiome predominantly includes gram-positive bacteria, with aerobic *Corynebacterium* species playing a key role in odor production.</mark> <mark>These bacteria metabolize apocrine gland secretions, generating volatile compounds such as **16-androstenes**, **5α-androstenol**, and **5α-androstenone**, which are known contributors to unpleasant odor.</mark>

<mark>Bacterial action also produces **ammonia** and **short-chain fatty acids**.</mark> <mark>The most well-characterized of these is **(S)-3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid**, a major component responsible for the characteristic axillary odor.</mark> <mark>The precise biotransformation pathways of these steroids and fatty acids remain incompletely understood and require further investigation.</mark>

# <mark>Clinical Findings and Diagnosis: Cutaneous Manifestations of Estrogen Excess and Deficiency</mark>

<mark>Estrogen exerts both beneficial and adverse cutaneous effects.</mark> <mark>In post-menopausal women, estrogen replacement therapy can reverse epidermal atrophy and restore cutaneous collagen.</mark> Estrogen's inhibitory effect on sebum production contributes to the improvement of acne seen with oral contraceptive therapy, particularly formulations with higher estrogenic activity. <mark>However, despite elevated estriol levels during pregnancy, the relative androgen excess—driven in part by progesterone's ability to bind androgen receptors—can exacerbate acne in some individuals.</mark>

<mark>Telogen effluvium, characterized by diffuse shedding of scalp or body hair, may occur postpartum or following discontinuation of oral contraceptives.</mark> <mark>Both pregnant women and those taking synthetic estrogens are more susceptible to estrogen-related side effects, including telangiectasias, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, and pigmentary changes.</mark>

<mark>Melanocytic lesions such as preexisting nevi and malignant melanoma may darken during pregnancy.</mark> <mark>Hyperpigmentation commonly affects the nipples, linea nigra, and genitalia.</mark> <mark>**Melasma**, often termed the "mask of pregnancy," presents as irregular, hyperpigmented patches on the forehead, cheeks, nose, upper lip, chin, and neck.</mark> <mark>Although melasma may improve after delivery, it often recurs in subsequent pregnancies.</mark> <mark>When induced by oral contraceptives, melasma can persist even after stopping the medication.</mark>

<mark>**Acanthosis nigricans** may be associated with estrogen excess.</mark> <mark>In conditions with elevated estrogen levels—such as pregnancy or oral contraceptive use—increased hair growth on the face, breasts, and extremities may occur.</mark> <mark>This is likely due to the complex interaction between estrogens and androgenic hormones rather than a direct stimulatory effect of estrogen on hair follicles.</mark>

<mark>**Estrogen and progesterone dermatitis** is a rare condition characterized by a polymorphous, cyclical eruption that flares pre-menstrually and may include pruritus.</mark> <mark>Diagnosis can be supported by intradermal testing with estrogen and progesterone, with observation for erythema or wheal formation within 15 to 60 minutes.</mark> <mark>Oral contraceptives have also been linked to **erythema nodosum**.</mark>

Estrogen deficiency—due to menopause, pituitary failure, or medications such as danazol, leuprolide, or clomiphene citrate—can lead to hot flashes, genital epithelial atrophy, and decreased breast size. Flushing episodes, marked by intense heat lasting several minutes, may also occur in younger women during the late luteal phase when estrogen levels are lowest.

# Treatment

The Pigmentary Disorders Academy recommends fixed "triple-ingredient" combinations as first-line therapy for melasma. Topical treatments commonly used include retinoids, corticosteroids, azelaic acid, and hydroquinone-based bleaching agents.

**Kligman's formula**, developed in 1975, is the classic triple-combination preparation containing:
- 5% hydroquinone (a depigmenting agent),
- 0.1% tretinoin (a retinoid that enhances epidermal turnover),
- 0.1% dexamethasone (a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation).

This formulation is typically compounded in a hydrophilic ointment base. Dual-ingredient combinations or single-agent therapies are acceptable alternatives when triple therapy is not tolerated or contraindicated.

## Hyperpigmentation in Thyrotoxicosis

The occurrence of hyperpigmentation in thyrotoxic patients has been estimated to range from 2 percent to as high as 40 percent in large series. The increased cutaneous pigmentation can be localized or generalized and is more common in individuals with darker skin. The distribution often resembles that seen in Addison disease, with pigment deposition in the creases of the palms and soles. However, several distinguishing features exist: mucous membrane involvement is uncommon, and pigmentation of the nipples and genital skin is less pronounced.

Hyperpigmentation associated with thyrotoxicosis is thought to result from increased release of pituitary ACTH, which compensates for accelerated cortisol degradation. The response of hyperpigmentation to treatment for hyperthyroidism is generally poor. Autoimmune Graves disease has also been reported in association with vitiligo.

## <mark>Melasma</mark>

<mark>Melasma is a common hypermelanosis that typically affects sun-exposed areas of the face.</mark> <mark>Its pathogenesis is not fully understood, but genetic and hormonal factors, in combination with UV radiation, play important roles.</mark> <mark>Specific precipitating factors include:</mark>

- <mark>Oral contraceptives</mark>  
- <mark>Estrogen replacement therapy</mark>  
- <mark>Mild ovarian or thyroid dysfunction</mark>  
- <mark>Ovarian tumors</mark>  
- <mark>Cosmetics</mark>  
- <mark>Nutritional factors</mark>  
- <mark>Phototoxic and photoallergic medications</mark>  
- <mark>Antiepileptic drugs</mark>  

<mark>Melasma is rarely reported before puberty and is significantly more common in women, especially those of reproductive age.</mark> <mark>Individuals with darker skin types (Fitzpatrick types IV, V, or VI) are more frequently affected.</mark>

<mark>Lesions appear as brownish macules with irregular borders and a symmetric facial distribution, often coalescing into a reticular pattern.</mark> <mark>Sun exposure exacerbates the condition.</mark> <mark>Three major patterns of distribution are recognized:</mark>

- <mark>**Centrofacial (63%)**: forehead, nose, chin, and upper lip</mark>  
- <mark>**Malar (21%)**: cheeks and nose</mark>  
- <mark>**Mandibular (16%)**: ramus of the mandible</mark>  

<mark>The anterior chest and dorsal forearms may also be involved.</mark>

<mark>Under Wood's lamp examination, melasma is classically categorized as epidermal, dermal, or mixed.</mark> <mark>The epidermal type shows sharp borders and enhanced visibility under Wood's lamp, while the dermal or mixed type appears blotchy and is less apparent.</mark> <mark>In most cases, melanin is distributed in the basal layer of the epidermis and the dermis.</mark>

<mark>Sun exposure is a major contributing factor, and sun protection is essential in management.</mark> <mark>Epidermal pigmentation tends to respond better to topical treatments than dermal pigmentation.</mark> <mark>Effective hypopigmenting agents include:</mark>

- <mark>Hydroquinone</mark>  
- <mark>Tretinoin cream</mark>  
- <mark>Azelaic acid</mark>  
- Rucinol  
- <mark>Kojic acid</mark>  

<mark>The Kligman formula—a combination of hydroquinone, tretinoin, and a weak topical corticosteroid—is widely used.</mark> <mark>Chemical peels and laser therapy may be beneficial but carry a risk of inducing further hyperpigmentation.</mark> <mark>In some cases, melasma gradually resolves after withdrawal of hormonal triggers and with strict sun avoidance.</mark>

## Pigmentation Changes in Pregnancy

During pregnancy, increased pigmentation occurs in approximately 90% of women and is more pronounced in those with darker skin types. Pre-existing pigmented lesions such as nevi and ephelides often darken, and recent scars may also become hyperpigmented. Normally pigmented areas—including the nipples, areolae, and genitalia—typically exhibit intensified coloration.

The linea alba, the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, frequently becomes hyperpigmented during pregnancy and is then referred to as **linea nigra**. A small proportion of pregnant women develop hyperpigmentation in the axillae or inner upper thighs.

Melasma, commonly known as the "mask of pregnancy," affects more than 50% of pregnant women.

## <mark>Acanthosis Nigricans</mark>

Acanthosis nigricans is a condition characterized by hyperpigmentation and velvety thickening of the skin, typically in intertriginous areas. It is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and endocrinopathies, and is discussed in detail in Chapters 152 and 154.

## Diabetes and Skin Pigmentation

(See Chapter on Diabetes)

# Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis: European expert consensus for diagnosis and management

## Abstract

**Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)** is a rare, usually drug-induced, acute pustular rash. Despite the lack of strong evidence supporting the efficacy of topical or systemic corticosteroids in this condition, they are commonly used. There is currently no consensus on the diagnostic approach or management of AGEP. This paper presents European expert recommendations for the diagnosis and management of AGEP.

The ToxiTEN group of the European Reference Network (ERN)-Skin—comprising dermatologists and allergologists with expertise in drug reactions—developed these recommendations based on clinical experience and a review of the literature. The recommendations are organized into four categories: professionals involved, diagnosis of AGEP, patient management, and allergological evaluation after the acute phase.

Consensus was reached on key aspects including the multidisciplinary team required, minimum diagnostic work-up, treatment setting, therapeutic interventions, and the timing and methods of allergological follow-up. A multidisciplinary approach involving dermatologists, allergologists, and pharmacovigilance services is strongly recommended.

## Background and Current Knowledge

<mark>**Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)** is a rare, typically drug-induced, severe cutaneous adverse reaction characterized by an acute pustular eruption.</mark> <mark>The estimated incidence ranges from 1 to 5 cases per million per year.</mark> <mark>The prognosis is generally excellent, with a mortality rate below 5%.</mark> <mark>AGEP primarily affects adults, with a median age of onset around 60 years, and shows a female predominance.</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

<mark>AGEP presents with the sudden onset of **widespread erythema**, predominantly in intertriginous areas (e.g., axillae, groin), accompanied by numerous **pinpoint, non-follicular, sterile pustules**.</mark> <mark>Fever is almost always present.</mark> <mark>Additional cutaneous manifestations may include:</mark>

- <mark>Facial edema</mark>  
- <mark>Purpuric lesions</mark>  
- <mark>Atypical target-like lesions</mark>  
- <mark>Vesicles</mark>  
- <mark>Rarely, bullae</mark>  

<mark>Pustules may coalesce, leading to superficial epidermal detachment resembling a **pseudo-Nikolsky sign**.</mark> <mark>Mucosal involvement occurs in less than 20% of cases and is typically limited to the oral mucosa.</mark>

### <mark>Systemic Involvement</mark>

<mark>Systemic complications occur in approximately 17% of patients and may involve:</mark>

- <mark>Liver (most common)</mark>  
- Kidneys  
- <mark>Bone marrow</mark>  
- <mark>Lungs (rare)</mark>  

<mark>Hemodynamic instability, including hypotension or shock, is reported in 22% of cases.</mark> <mark>These features raise the possibility of overlap with other severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as **drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)** or, less commonly, **toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)**.</mark>

### <mark>Laboratory Findings</mark>

<mark>Common laboratory abnormalities include:</mark>

- <mark>**Leukocytosis with neutrophilia**</mark>  
- <mark>**Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP)**</mark>  
- <mark>**Mild eosinophilia** (in 30–50% of cases)</mark>  

### Diagnosis

The **EuroSCAR scoring system** is a validated tool to assess the likelihood of AGEP and differentiate it from other pustular eruptions.

Skin biopsy is essential for confirmation. Histopathology typically shows:

- **Spongiform subcorneal or intraepidermal pustules**  
- **Edematous papillary dermis**  
- **Perivascular inflammatory infiltrate** rich in neutrophils, with some eosinophils  

Occasionally, necrotic keratinocytes or leucocytoclastic vasculitis may be seen.

### Differential Diagnosis

The main differential diagnosis is **generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP)**. Histological clues favoring GPP include:

- Psoriasiform acanthosis  
- Papillomatosis  
- Tortuous or dilated capillaries  

A personal or family history of psoriasis is present in 7–10% of AGEP cases, complicating the distinction between AGEP and GPP.

### Special Considerations

- **Localized exanthematous pustulosis (ALEP)** has been described, particularly with topical medications, though its pathogenesis remains unclear.  
- Comorbidities such as diabetes, renal failure, prior psoriasis, and history of hypersensitivity reactions are frequently reported in AGEP patients.  
- AGEP patients may have a higher body mass index compared to those with DRESS.  

A multidisciplinary approach is essential for accurate diagnosis, appropriate management, and pharmacovigilance reporting.

## Superantigens and T-Cell Activation

Unlike conventional peptide antigens, whose recognition by the T-cell receptor (TCR) is restricted by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) alleles, superantigens are generally **not MHC restricted**. Instead, superantigens bind directly to the **variable region of the TCR β chain (Vβ)**, bypassing the need for processing and presentation via the typical antigen-presenting pathway. In contrast, nominal peptide antigens require recognition by all five variable elements of the TCR—**Vβ, Dβ, Jβ, Vα, and Jα**—resulting in a much more limited pool of responsive T cells.

Because superantigens engage only the Vβ domain, they can activate a significantly larger proportion of T cells. The frequency of T-cell response to superantigens ranges from **20% to 30%**, compared to only **0.01% to 0.1%** for conventional peptide antigens. This broad activation occurs because superantigens simultaneously bind to **MHC class II molecules** on antigen-presenting cells and to the **Vβ region** of the TCR, effectively cross-linking and activating a large population of T cells.

This massive T-cell activation leads to the generation of increased numbers of **cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA)-positive T cells**, which are predisposed to migrate to the skin. The predominance of CLA-positive T cells helps explain the frequent **cutaneous manifestations** observed in superantigen-mediated diseases.

## Cytokine Storm and Clinical Manifestations

Superantigen-driven T-cell activation results in a **profound cytokine release**, including **tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)**, **interleukin-1 (IL-1)**, and **interleukin-6 (IL-6)**. This "cytokine storm" is a key driver of systemic inflammation and contributes to **capillary leak syndrome**, leading to hypotension, edema, and multiorgan dysfunction. These effects underlie the severe clinical features seen in superantigen-mediated conditions.

The prototypical example is **toxic shock syndrome (TSS)**, most commonly caused by exotoxins from *Staphylococcus aureus* or **group A streptococcus (GAS)**. While distinct syndromes such as **TSS** and **scarlet fever** have characteristic features, overlapping clinical presentations are common. This variability reflects differences in **toxin type, quantity**, and the **host immune response**.

## Classification of Superantigen-Mediated Disorders

Superantigen-mediated diseases can be categorized based on the degree of systemic involvement:

- **Predominantly systemic**: Includes **toxic shock syndrome (TSS)** and **scarlet fever**, both associated with significant systemic toxicity.
- **Intermediate cutaneous and systemic**: Includes conditions such as **recalcitrant erythematous desquamating disorder (REDD)** and **toxin-mediated erythema**, which represent milder, less systemic forms of TSS and scarlet fever, respectively.

All these disorders are diagnosed **clinically** and may be caused by toxins from either *S. aureus* or **group A streptococcus**.

---

## <mark>Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)</mark>

<mark>TSS is a severe inflammatory condition characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>High fever</mark>
- <mark>Diffuse macular rash</mark>
- <mark>Hypotension</mark>
- <mark>Multiorgan dysfunction</mark>

<mark>It represents the most severe end of the spectrum of superantigen-mediated diseases.</mark>

### Historical Background

First described in 1978 in children with *S. aureus* infections, TSS gained widespread attention in the early 1980s due to outbreaks linked to **highly absorbent tampon use** in menstruating women. The tampon provided a favorable environment for bacterial growth by neutralizing the acidic vaginal pH and supplying nutrients via menstrual blood.

Since then, removal of these tampons from the market and public health education have led to a **decline in menstrual-associated TSS**. Currently, **non-menstrual TSS** is more common and associated with various staphylococcal infections, including wound infections, post-surgical infections, and respiratory tract infections.

### Clinical Findings: Staphylococcal TSS

The primary toxin responsible for TSS is **TSS toxin-1 (TSST-1)**, which is implicated in most **menstrual-associated cases**. TSST-1 is unique among superantigens in its ability to **cross mucosal barriers**, facilitating systemic absorption.

Despite reductions in incidence, TSS remains a medical emergency requiring prompt recognition and treatment. Both staphylococcal and streptococcal forms can lead to life-threatening complications due to overwhelming immune activation and cytokine release.

## <mark>Staphylococcal Scarlet Fever</mark>

<mark>The exanthem of staphylococcal scarlet fever tends to be more tender than that seen in streptococcal scarlet fever.</mark> <mark>Systemic signs such as malaise and fever are invariably present.</mark> Within a few days of rash onset, thick desquamation begins, and the entire skin may peel over the following week.

<mark>Unlike generalized staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), the scarlatina-form eruption is not associated with bullae or superficial epidermal exfoliation and can be clinically challenging to distinguish from other infectious erythrodermal conditions such as toxic shock syndrome (TSS) and streptococcal scarlet fever.</mark> <mark>A key distinguishing feature of staphylococcal scarlet fever is the absence of pharyngitis, which is typically present in streptococcal-mediated disease.</mark> Instead, the infection usually originates from a cutaneous focus.

A study by Wang and colleagues evaluated 20 children with staphylococcal scarlet fever. All infections originated from the skin: 16 cases from furuncles or carbuncles, and 2 each from abscesses or wound infections. All *Staphylococcus aureus* isolates expressed staphylococcal enterotoxin B (SEB). Notably, SEB shares significant protein sequence homology with streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A (SPEA), a toxin linked to streptococcal scarlet fever. However, other studies have implicated additional staphylococcal enterotoxins in similar cases. This variability in toxin profiles may reflect the clinical basis of diagnosis. It has been proposed that staphylococcal scarlet fever may represent an incomplete form of TSS, where toxins spread from a skin source, preferentially activating skin-associated lymphoid tissue rather than mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue.

Given that streptococcal scarlet fever typically follows pharyngitis, the presence of a scarlet fever–like rash without pharyngitis should prompt evaluation for a localized skin infection (e.g., furuncle) that can be cultured to confirm the diagnosis.

## Differential Diagnosis

The diagnosis of scarlet fever is primarily clinical and supported by positive bacterial cultures. <mark>The differential diagnosis includes other toxin-mediated conditions such as SSSS.</mark>

- **Kawasaki disease** shares features such as mucosal changes (e.g., strawberry tongue), extremity swelling, and palmoplantar desquamation during recovery. However, Kawasaki disease is characterized by prolonged fever and negative bacterial cultures.
- **Atypical drug hypersensitivity reactions** may mimic some cutaneous findings but lack mucosal involvement. These reactions are typically associated with a history of recent drug exposure and peripheral eosinophilia.
- **Streptococcal vs. staphylococcal scarlet fever**: Streptococcal cases usually arise from pharyngitis, whereas staphylococcal cases originate from a skin infection.

## Treatment and Prognosis

Treatment involves antibiotics to eliminate the causative organism. If a localized skin infection (e.g., abscess, furuncle, or carbuncle) is present, incision and drainage are essential. Unlike streptococcal scarlet fever, staphylococcal scarlet fever is not associated with acute rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. In cases with systemic features resembling TSS, management should follow TSS treatment guidelines.

---

## Recurrent Toxin-Mediated Perineal Erythema

In 1996, Manders and colleagues described a novel condition termed **recurrent toxin-mediated perineal erythema**. This disorder is characterized by a sudden onset of striking, diffuse macular erythema in the perineal area, appearing 24 to 48 hours after pharyngitis caused by toxin-producing group A *Streptococcus* or *S. aureus*.

Clinical features often overlap with scarlet fever and may include:
- Strawberry tongue
- Perineal erythema and edema
- Subsequent palmoplantar desquamation

Notably, systemic signs such as high fever, hypotension, or other manifestations of TSS or scarlet fever are typically absent. Diarrhea is a common accompanying symptom. Recurrences are more frequent in this localized variant compared to classic scarlet fever.

# <mark>European guidelines for topical photodynamic therapy part 1: treatment delivery and current indications – actinic keratoses, Bowen's disease, basal cell carcinoma</mark>

## <mark>Abstract</mark>

<mark>Topical photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a widely used non-invasive treatment for certain non-melanoma skin cancers, allowing for the treatment of large and multiple lesions with excellent cosmetic outcomes.</mark> High efficacy has been demonstrated for PDT using standardized protocols in non-hyperkeratotic actinic keratoses (AK), Bowen's disease (BD), superficial basal cell carcinomas (BCC), and certain thin nodular BCCs, with superior cosmetic results compared to conventional therapies. Recurrence rates following PDT are generally comparable to those of other non-surgical treatments, although they are higher than after surgical excision for nodular BCC. PDT is not recommended for invasive squamous cell carcinoma. The treatment is usually well tolerated, but tingling, discomfort, or pain during illumination is common. Recent studies have identified patient factors associated with increased pain, enabling earlier implementation of pain-minimization strategies. Reduced discomfort has been observed with newer protocols, including shorter photosensitizer application times and daylight PDT for actinic keratoses.

## Introduction

These guidelines aim to promote safe and effective practice across Europe for the delivery of topical photodynamic therapy (PDT) in dermatological conditions. They are based on evidence from a systematic literature review (using MEDLINE) and previous clinical guidelines. A companion paper (Part II) reviews emerging and novel indications for topical PDT.

To date, topical PDT has been approved for the treatment of selected non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC). Currently, only three photosensitizing agents are licensed for use in Europe (see Table 1):

- **Methyl aminolaevulinate (MAL)** – marketed as Metvix®/Metvixia® (Galerma, Lausanne, Switzerland) – used with red light for non-hyperkeratotic actinic keratoses (AK), Bowen's disease (BD), superficial BCC, and nodular BCC, though approvals vary by country.
- **5-ALA patch** – Alacare® (Spirig AG, Egerkingen, Switzerland) – approved for mild AK in a single session with red light, without lesion preparation.
- **BF-200 ALA** – Ameluz® (Biofrontera AG, Leverkusen, Germany) – licensed for use with red light in PDT.

Another formulation, **Levulan** (5-ALA; DUSA Pharmaceuticals, Wilmington, MA, USA), is approved in North America and some other regions for AK, using a blue light activation protocol. Many early studies used non-standardized, hospital-prepared formulations of aminolaevulinic acid (ALA), which limits direct comparison between study outcomes.

## Photosensitizers

Topical photodynamic therapy, first described over two decades ago, involves the application of a photosensitizer prodrug—typically aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) or its methyl ester MAL. These compounds are metabolized via the heme biosynthesis pathway into protoporphyrin IX (PpIX), which, when activated by light of an appropriate wavelength, generates reactive oxygen species—particularly singlet oxygen—leading to apoptosis and necrosis of targeted cells.

<mark>Selective accumulation in lesional tissue is attributed to altered permeability of the stratum corneum and differences in porphyrin metabolism in diseased cells.</mark> Photosensitizer uptake may also occur in activated lymphocytes within the lesion.

ALA is hydrophilic, while MAL is more lipophilic, potentially allowing deeper penetration into skin lesions. However, comparative studies in AK and nodular BCC have not consistently shown superior efficacy of one agent over the other.

Recent data show that **BF-200 ALA**, a nanoemulsion formulation designed to enhance stability and skin penetration, achieved higher complete clearance rates than MAL in the treatment of thin to moderate facial and scalp AK: **78% vs. 64%**, respectively.

A self-adhesive, skin-colored 5-ALA patch applied directly to AK lesions—without crust removal—demonstrated superior efficacy compared to cryotherapy in clearing mild to moderate AK.

Techniques such as iontophoresis or chemical enhancers to improve photosensitizer penetration may increase PDT efficacy but remain experimental and are not yet part of routine clinical practice.

# <mark>Topical and Intralesional Cytotoxic Agents</mark>

## <mark>5-FLUOROURACIL</mark>

### <mark>Mechanism of Action and Formulations</mark>

<mark>Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) has been used in clinical practice since the 1960s.</mark> It is a structural analogue of thymine that blocks DNA synthesis by inhibiting thymidylate synthetase. <mark>Topical 5-FU is commercially available as a 0.5 percent cream carried in a microsphere vehicle, as a 1 percent solution or 1 percent cream, as a 2 percent or 5 percent solution, and as a 5 percent cream.</mark> The solution can also be used for intralesional injection.

### Indications

<mark>5-FU 5 percent cream has been approved by the U.S.</mark> Food and Drug Administration (FDA) since 1970 for the treatment of actinic keratoses in any location; 5-FU 0.5 percent cream is FDA approved for treatment of actinic keratoses of the face and anterior scalp. 5-FU is used twice daily until an inflammatory response is seen, usually 2 to 4 weeks. The 0.5 percent cream can be used once daily. 5-FU may also be a useful adjunct before cryosurgery of actinic keratoses. Pre-treatment with a keratolytic agent, prolonged therapy, more frequent applications, or the use of occlusive dressings may increase therapeutic response.

### Treatment Considerations

Irritation during treatment sometimes requires reduction or interruption of treatment and the addition of emollients or topical corticosteroids to help quell brisk inflammation. A number of approaches to decrease irritation have been devised; whether or not efficacy is preserved is disputed. Weekly pulse dosing involves applying the medication for 1 to 2 days per week for 6 to 7 weeks. Use of the 0.5 percent 5-FU cream with microsphere vehicle may allow for a more tolerable irritation profile.

During 5-FU treatment, previously sub-clinical actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas, and squamous cell carcinomas may respond to treatment and become apparent. <mark>In fact, the 5 percent 5-FU cream is approved by the FDA for the treatment of superficial basal cell carcinomas.</mark> Verrucae vulgaris, verrucae plana, plantar warts, and condylomata acuminata have been treated with varying response rates with topical and intralesional 5-FU. Additionally, actinic cheilitis, mucosal leukoplakia, radiodermatitis, Bowen disease, Bowenoid papulosis, and erythroplasia of Queyrat have all been reported to respond to treatment with topical 5-FU. Further, there are reports of the successful treatment of both psoriasis and keratoacanthomas with topical and intralesional 5-FU, and of infantile digital fibromatosis treated with intralesional 5-FU. Intralesional 5-FU has also been reported to be effective in the treatment of keloids and hypertrophic scars.

The systemic absorption of topically applied 5-FU is limited, with absorption selectively greater from abnormal skin than from surrounding normal skin. Microsphere-based formulations may retain 5-FU at the target site, with less drug reaching the systemic circulation. Rarely, systemic effects of 5-FU include nausea and anorexia, stomatitis, diarrhea, myelosuppression, alopecia, and cardiac and neurologic toxicity. Side effects of the topical preparation include local irritation, erythema, pain, swelling, pruritus, dyspigmentation, allergic contact dermatitis, and photosensitivity. Unusual reactions may include onycholysis, onychodystrophy, and the appearance of telangiectasias. The use of injectable preparations may be complicated by pain, local ulceration, erosion, desquamation, and dyspigmentation.

## MECHLORETHAMINE (NITROGEN MUSTARD)

### Mechanism of Action and Formulations

Mechlorethamine [methyl-bis (2-chloroethyl) amine hydrochloride] was the first nitrogen mustard (NM) to be used in clinical medicine.

# <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- <mark>**Inheritance**: X-linked recessive</mark>  
- **Gene**: Mutations in *WAS* (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome gene)  
- <mark>**Classic clinical triad**:</mark>  
  <mark>- Recalcitrant dermatitis</mark>  
  <mark>- Recurrent pyogenic infections</mark>  
  <mark>- Hemorrhage due to thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction</mark>  
- **Therapy**: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone marrow transplantation)

---

## Immunological Features

Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) exhibit multiple immune cell defects, including:  
- <mark>Impaired **NK cell cytotoxicity**</mark>  
- <mark>Defective **dendritic cell migration and activation**</mark>  
- <mark>**Impaired macrophage chemotaxis**</mark>

<mark>These contribute to the broad susceptibility to infections and immune dysregulation seen in the disease.</mark>

---

## <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

<mark>The classic triad of hemorrhage, recurrent pyogenic infections, and recalcitrant dermatitis is present in only **25% of patients**.</mark> However, individual manifestations are common:

### <mark>Bleeding Diathesis</mark>
- <mark>Present in **84% of patients**, making it the most frequent manifestation</mark>  
- <mark>Typically appears in the **first weeks or months of life**</mark>  
- <mark>Common presentations:</mark>  
  <mark>- Bloody diarrhea (often initial sign)</mark>  
  <mark>- Epistaxis</mark>  
  <mark>- Hematemesis</mark>  
  <mark>- Hematuria</mark>  
  <mark>- Mucocutaneous petechiae</mark>  
  - Intracranial hemorrhage  

<mark>Thrombocytopenia is **persistent**, with platelet counts ranging from **1,000 to 80,000/μL**.</mark>  
- <mark>**Diagnostic criterion**: Platelet count < **70,000/μL**</mark>  
- <mark>Platelets are characteristically **small (microthrombocytopenia)**</mark>  
- Platelet aggregation is defective

---

### <mark>Infections</mark>
- <mark>Recurrent **bacterial infections** begin in infancy as maternal antibodies wane</mark>  
- <mark>Common infections:</mark>  
  <mark>- Furunculosis</mark>  
  <mark>- Conjunctivitis</mark>  
  <mark>- Otitis media and externa</mark>  
  <mark>- Pansinusitis</mark>  
  <mark>- Pneumonia</mark>  
  - Meningitis  
  <mark>- Septicemia</mark>  

- <mark>Predominant pathogens: **Encapsulated bacteria**</mark>  
  <mark>- *Streptococcus pneumoniae*</mark>  
  <mark>- *Haemophilus influenzae*</mark>  
  <mark>- *Neisseria meningitidis*</mark>  

- <mark>Increased susceptibility to:</mark>  
  <mark>- Herpesviruses and other viruses</mark>  
  <mark>- *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (formerly *P. carinii*)</mark>

---

### <mark>Dermatitis</mark>
- <mark>Occurs in **~80% of patients**</mark>  
- <mark>Typically develops in the **first few months of life**</mark>  
- <mark>Often **severe and widespread**</mark>  
- <mark>Commonly affects:</mark>  
  - Face  
  - Scalp  
  <mark>- Flexural areas</mark>  

- Features distinguishing it from typical atopic dermatitis:  
  <mark>- More **exfoliative**</mark>  
  <mark>- **Serosanguineous crusting**</mark>  
  - Frequent **lichenification**  

- Complications:  
  <mark>- Secondary bacterial infection</mark>  
  <mark>- **Eczema herpeticum**</mark>  
  - **Molluscum contagiosum**  

- Additional IgE-mediated conditions:  
  <mark>- Urticaria</mark>  
  <mark>- Food allergies</mark>  
  - Asthma

---

### Autoimmune Manifestations
- <mark>Occur in **up to 40% of patients**</mark>  
- Most common:  
  <mark>- **Vasculitis** (20%) – affecting skin, GI tract, brain, heart</mark>  
  <mark>- **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia** (14%)</mark>  
  - **IgA nephropathy** (up to 10%)  

- Other immune-mediated conditions:  
  - Angioedema  
  - Dermatomyositis  
  - Pyoderma gangrenosum  
  - Erythema nodosum  

- Hepatosplenomegaly is common  
- Lymphadenopathy, transient arthritis, and joint effusions may occur

---

## Laboratory Findings

- **Thrombocytopenia** with **small platelets**  
- **Immunoglobulin abnormalities**:  
  - ↓ IgM (common)  
  - ↓ IgG (sometimes)  
  - Absent isohemagglutinins  
  - ↑ IgA, IgE, IgD  

- Impaired humoral and cellular immunity contributes to infection susceptibility and autoimmunity

--- 

*Note: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy and is recommended early in the disease course.*

# Differential Diagnosis of Atopic Dermatitis

## Most Likely
- Contact dermatitis (allergic and irritant)  
- Seborrheic dermatitis  
- Scabies  
- Psoriasis  
- Ichthyosis vulgaris  
- Keratosis pilaris  
- Dermatophytosis  

## Consider
- Asteatotic eczema  
- Lichen simplex chronicus  
- Nummular dermatitis  
- Juvenile palmar-plantar dermatosis  
- Impetigo  
- Drug eruptions  
- Perioral dermatitis  
- Pityriasis alba  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  
- Molluscum dermatitis  

## Less Common/Rare Disorders Predominantly in Adolescents and Adults
- Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or Sézary syndrome)  
- Human immunodeficiency virus–associated dermatoses  
- Lupus erythematosus  
- Dermatomyositis  
- Graft-versus-host disease  
- Pemphigus foliaceus  
- Dermatitis herpetiformis  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  

## Complications

### Ocular Problems
Eye complications associated with severe atopic dermatitis can lead to significant morbidity. Eyelid dermatitis and chronic blepharitis are commonly seen and may result in visual impairment due to corneal scarring. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is typically bilateral and can cause disabling symptoms such as itching, burning, tearing, and copious mucoid discharge.

---

<mark>Infants presenting in the first year of life with failure to thrive, diarrhea, generalized scaling erythematous rash, and recurrent cutaneous or systemic infections should be evaluated for severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome.</mark> <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder, presents with cutaneous findings nearly indistinguishable from atopic dermatitis.</mark> <mark>It is associated with thrombocytopenia, variable abnormalities in humoral and cellular immunity, and recurrent severe bacterial infections.</mark>

<mark>Hyper-IgE syndrome is characterized by elevated serum IgE levels, defective T-cell function, and recurrent deep-seated bacterial infections, including cutaneous abscesses caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or pruritic skin disease due to *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* pustulosis, or recalcitrant dermatophytosis.</mark> <mark>A papulopustular eruption on the face and scalp may appear in early life.</mark> <mark>Although *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* is a major pathogen, infections with other bacteria, viruses, and fungi may occur—especially in patients on long-term anti-staphylococcal antibiotic prophylaxis.</mark> <mark>Additional features include pneumonia with pneumatocele formation, dental anomalies with retained primary teeth, bone fractures, and osteopenia.</mark>

It is important to recognize that adults presenting with eczematous dermatitis without a history of childhood eczema, respiratory allergy, or atopic family history may have allergic contact dermatitis. A contact allergen should be suspected in any patient whose dermatitis fails to respond to appropriate therapy. Notably, contact allergy to topical glucocorticoids and topical calcineurin inhibitors has been reported in patients with chronic dermatitis. Additionally, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma must be ruled out in adults with chronic, treatment-resistant dermatitis. Skin biopsies should ideally be obtained from three separate sites, as histology may show spongiosis and inflammatory infiltrate resembling atopic dermatitis.

Eczematous dermatitis has also been reported in association with human immunodeficiency virus infection and various infestations, such as scabies. Other conditions that may mimic atopic dermatitis include psoriasis, ichthyoses, and seborrheic dermatitis.

# Guidelines for Treatment of Atopic Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) – Part I

## Abstract

The evidence for the treatment of atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis, AE) is evaluated according to the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE) instrument. The consensus process included a nominal group technique and a DELPHI procedure. Management of AE must account for the individual variability in symptoms and disease course.

**Basic therapy** centers on regular use of hydrating topical agents and avoidance of specific and non-specific triggering factors. For flare-ups, **anti-inflammatory treatment** with topical glucocorticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs) is recommended. TCIs (tacrolimus and pimecrolimus) are increasingly used not only for exacerbations but also for proactive therapy in selected cases, particularly in sensitive areas such as the face and neck.

Topical corticosteroids remain the first-line anti-inflammatory treatment. However, TCIs are preferred in certain anatomical locations due to lower risk of skin atrophy. For severe, refractory cases, **systemic immunosuppressive therapy** may be considered.

Microbial colonization—especially by *Staphylococcus aureus*—and superinfection can trigger flares and may warrant adjunctive antimicrobial treatment. **Phototherapy**, particularly with UVA1 or narrowband UVB (311 nm), is an effective adjuvant option.

Dietary interventions should be implemented only in cases of confirmed food allergy. **Allergen-specific immunotherapy** to aeroallergens may benefit selected patients. Psychological stress can exacerbate AE, making **psychosomatic counseling** advisable in some cases. Structured patient education programs, such as **"eczema schools"**, have demonstrated efficacy.

Pruritus is a central symptom targeted by most therapies, but some patients require additional **antipruritic treatments**.

## Introduction

Atopic eczema (AE), also known as atopic dermatitis, eczema, or *Neurodermitis* in German-speaking countries, is a chronic or chronically relapsing, inflammatory, and intensely pruritic skin disorder. It frequently occurs in families with a history of other atopic conditions, such as bronchial asthma or allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

AE is one of the most prevalent skin diseases worldwide, affecting up to **20% of children** and **1–3% of adults**. It often represents the initial stage of the "atopic march," preceding the development of allergic rhinitis and asthma.

Diagnosis of AE relies on established clinical criteria. There is no pathognomonic laboratory biomarker. While elevated total or allergen-specific IgE levels and positive skin prick tests are common, they are not universal. Patients without IgE sensitization are classified as having **intrinsic (non-IgE-associated) AE**, in contrast to the **extrinsic (IgE-associated) form**. This distinction remains debated but has practical implications for management, particularly regarding allergen avoidance strategies.

### Aetiopathophysiology

The development of AE involves a complex interplay of genetic, immunological, and environmental factors:

- **Genetic predisposition**: High heritability is evident, with 80% concordance in monozygotic twins versus 20% in dizygotic twins.  
- **Immune dysregulation**: Early disease stages are characterized by a Th2-dominant immune response, leading to increased IgE production.  
- **Skin barrier dysfunction**: Impaired barrier function results from abnormalities in lipid composition and structural proteins, including filaggrin mutations and deficiency in protease inhibitors, contributing to dry skin and increased allergen penetration.  
- **Microbial dysbiosis**: Abnormal colonization with pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Malassezia furfur*, instead of commensals like *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, increases infection risk and inflammation.  
- **Psychosomatic factors**: Stress influences disease activity via autonomic nervous system imbalance and increased release of inflammatory mediators from cells such as eosinophils.

Effective management of AE requires an individualized approach that addresses the specific pathogenic mechanisms present in each patient.

### Disease Severity Assessment

After diagnosis, assessment of disease severity is essential. The **Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD)** index, developed by the European Task Force on Atopic Dermatitis (ETFAD), is the standard tool for evaluating extent, intensity, and subjective symptoms (pruritus and sleep disturbance).

## <mark>Pellagra</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>
5-Fluorouracil inhibits the conversion of tryptophan to niacin, and 6-mercaptopurine inhibits NAD phosphorylase, thereby impairing NAD production. Other medications associated with pellagra include phenytoin, chloramphenicol, azathioprine, sulfonamides, and antidepressants.

### <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>
<mark>Pellagra is classically characterized by the "four Ds": **dermatitis**, **diarrhea**, **dementia**, and **death**.</mark>

- <mark>**Dermatitis**: The rash is photosensitive and begins as erythematous, painful, or pruritic patches. Over several days, the skin becomes edematous and may develop vesicles and bullae that rupture, forming crusted erosions, or evolve into brown scales. Chronic changes include sharply demarcated, keratotic, hyperpigmented plaques.</mark>
  <mark>- Common sites: dorsum of the hands; when it extends proximally more on the radial than ulnar side, it forms the characteristic "gauntlet" of pellagra.</mark>
  <mark>- **Casal’s necklace**: A symmetric rash on the upper central chest and neck; may extend over the sternum as a "cravat."</mark>
  <mark>- Facial involvement may show a butterfly distribution across the nose, cheeks, chin, and lips.</mark>
  <mark>- Palms and soles may develop painful fissures resembling "goose skin."</mark>
  <mark>- Mucous membrane involvement includes cheilitis, angular stomatitis, glossitis, and ulcerations of the buccal mucosa and vulva.</mark>

- <mark>**Gastrointestinal symptoms**: Often early manifestations—diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia.</mark>

- <mark>**Neurologic symptoms**: Include insomnia, fatigue, nervousness, apathy, impaired memory, and depression. These may progress to psychosis and dementia in advanced stages.</mark>

- <mark>**Prognosis**: Untreated pellagra leads to death from multiorgan failure.</mark>

### Laboratory Testing
Diagnosis is primarily clinical and confirmed by rapid response to vitamin supplementation. Urinary metabolites such as **N-methylnicotinamide** and **pyridone** can be measured to support the diagnosis.

### Treatment
- Recommended daily intake: 15–20 mg of niacin or approximately 60 mg of exogenous tryptophan.
- Therapeutic dose: **500 mg/day** of **nicotinamide** or **nicotinic acid** for several weeks.
  - **Nicotinamide** is preferred due to fewer side effects (nicotinic acid commonly causes flushing and headache).
- Neuropsychiatric symptoms may improve within 24–48 hours.
- Skin lesions typically resolve over 3–4 weeks.

---

## Vitamin B₆ (Pyridoxine)

### Etiology and Pathogenesis
Vitamin **B₆** refers to three interconvertible forms: **pyridoxine**, **pyridoxamine**, and **pyridoxal**. Humans cannot synthesize these compounds and must obtain them from the diet.

- **Dietary sources**: Meats, whole grains, vegetables, and nuts are rich in vitamin B₆.
- **Absorption**: Occurs via passive diffusion in the jejunum.
- **Bioavailability**: Food processing can reduce available vitamin B₆.
- **Active form**: **Pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)** is the most common and physiologically active coenzyme form.
